source_catalog.authority: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1 (Definitions). 'Administer' means the direct application of a controlled substance whether by injection, inhalation, ingestion, or any other means to the body of a patient or research subject by -- (a) a practitioner, or (b) a nurse at the direction of a practitioner, or (c) a registered pharmacist acting in accordance with: (i) department regulations governing pharmacist administration of medications for treatment of mental health and substance use disorder and at the direction of a prescribing practitioner; (ii) a prescription for testosterone for gender-affirming care; or (iii) a prescription for the treatment and prevention of sexually transmitted infections or for the prevention of HIV; or (d) an ultimate user or research subject at the direction of a practitioner. The same section defines 'Dispense' as delivery to an ultimate user by or pursuant to the order of a practitioner, 'including the prescribing and administering of a controlled substance and the packaging, labeling, or compounding necessary for such delivery.'

M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 3(a)(6). Schedule VI comprises substances that are prescription drugs and that have not been included in Schedules I through V. This makes essentially every prescription medication in Massachusetts a 'controlled substance' for c. 94C purposes, so the s. 1 'Administer' definition and the Board's controlled-substance administration standard reach an ordinary prescription injectable.

247 CMR 9.00 (Professional Practice Standards), revision date 12/6/24. 247 CMR 9.01(1): a licensee shall conduct professional activities in conformity with M.G.L. c. 112, ss. 24 through 42D and M.G.L. c. 94C. 247 CMR 9.01(2): 'A licensee may not process a prescription; dispense a drug, device, or other substance; or administer a controlled substance or vaccine in a manner which is intended, either directly or indirectly, to circumvent any law or regulation governing the practice of pharmacy.' 247 CMR 9.01(4): 'A pharmacist shall practice pharmacy within the scope of his or her education, training, and experience and within the recognized pharmacist scope of practice.'

247 CMR 10.00 (Disciplinary Proceedings). 247 CMR 10.03(1): the Board may impose disciplinary action against 'an individual or entity licensed or registered by the Board' on the grounds in M.G.L. c. 112, s. 61 or on enumerated grounds including (b) violating M.G.L. c. 112, ss. 24 through 42A or any state or federal statute, rule or regulation related to the practice of the profession; (e) engaging in misconduct in the practice of the profession; (f) 'Engaging in conduct beyond the authorized scope of a pharmacist, pharmacy intern or pharmacy technician'; and (l) engaging in conduct that has the capacity or potential to deceive or defraud.

105 CMR 700.000 (Implementation of M.G.L. c. 94C). 105 CMR 700.001 defines 'Administer' with the same closed list of permitted administering parties, allowing a registered pharmacist or pharmacy intern to administer only 'medications for treatment of mental health or substance use disorders and at the direction of a prescribing practitioner.' 105 CMR 700.003 (Registration of Persons for a Specific Activity or Activities in Accordance with M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 7(g)), paragraph (6), separately provides that a registered pharmacist, pharmacy intern and pharmacy technician 'may dispense by administration influenza vaccine, COVID-19 vaccine, and other immunizations designated by the Department to persons five years of age or older,' subject to conditions. Together these confirm that Massachusetts pharmacist administration authority is enumerated and bounded rather than general.

247 CMR 2.00 (Definitions). Checked and recorded as a negative finding: the Board's own definitional chapter contains no definition of 'Administer,' which confirms that the controlling definition of the act of administration, and of who may perform it, is the M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1 / 105 CMR 700.001 definition rather than a separate Board definition.

ambiguity.note: The legal outcome is not in doubt. The only soft edge is that 247 CMR 9.01(2) is framed in terms of intent ('in a manner which is intended, either directly or indirectly, to circumvent'), so in principle a candidate could ask whether intent is established. The stem forecloses that by supplying facts whose only function is to negate any independent purpose for the handover: the patient is assigned no preparation, storage or handling role, no interval is set between handover and return, and the sequence runs identically for every patient. On those facts the handover is a pure formality and the circumvention intent is established. Separately, 247 CMR 9.01(4) (practice within the recognized pharmacist scope of practice) and 247 CMR 10.03(1)(f) (conduct beyond the authorized scope) bite regardless of intent, so the answer does not actually depend on resolving the intent question.

more_than_one_defensible_answer_set.note: C is uniquely correct. A, B, D and E are each defeated by identifiable authority rather than merely being less good: A by 247 CMR 9.01(2)'s express reach to indirect circumvention and by M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1, which defines 'Dispense' to include administering (so labelling the handover a completed dispensing does not detach the injection from the administration rules); B by the stem's own facts, since the pharmacist gives the injection and the c. 94C, s. 1(d) ultimate-user path requires the ultimate user to apply the substance to their own body; D by the closed enumeration in c. 94C, s. 1(c), under which a valid prescription and a lawful dispensing do not confer administration authority on a pharmacist outside the listed categories; and E by 247 CMR 10.03(1), which reaches 'an individual or entity licensed or registered by the Board' and lists conduct beyond the authorized pharmacist scope as its own ground.

stem_clarity.note: Readability is good: the choreography, the three pretext facts and the call ('Which assessment is best?') are unambiguous, and the pharmacist-asks-a-colleague framing is a clean single-best-answer setup. The reservation is substantive rather than linguistic. The stem stipulates the legal premise abstractly -- 'a medication that Massachusetts does not authorize a pharmacist to administer' -- instead of naming a medication and making the candidate determine, from M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1(c) and 105 CMR 700.003, whether it falls inside the enumerated categories. That is the actual Massachusetts-specific content, and the stem gives it away. What remains to be tested is a single general inference about sham sequencing, which is not jurisdiction-specific knowledge.

distractor_plausibility.note: Mixed. A is the strongest distractor and is genuinely attractive -- 'it was a completed dispensing, so the administration rules never engage' is exactly the formalist argument a corporate protocol author would advance, and a candidate who does not know 247 CMR 9.01(2) has no ready answer to it. D is a good distractor because conflating prescriptive/dispensing authority with administration authority is a real and common misconception. E is a fair distractor because 'responsibility sits with whoever wrote the protocol' is a real belief among staff pharmacists. B is weak: it is refuted by the stem itself, which says in terms that the pharmacist gives the injection, so a candidate can eliminate B on reading alone without any law. B functions as a near-dead option and effectively narrows the item toward a four-option question.

realistic_pharmacist_facing_character.note: The underlying situation is realistic and genuinely pharmacist-facing: chains do design service protocols centrally, those protocols do sometimes structure around a scope-of-practice limit, and a staff pharmacist asking 'is this actually allowed?' before the first clinic day is exactly the decision an MPJE candidate should be able to make. The execution is less realistic. The specific choreography -- patient carries the syringe to the consultation room and hands it back unopened -- is contrived, and no operator would commit that step to writing in the form described; a real evasion would be documented more opaquely. The stem also never names the medication or the restriction, which is atypical for the exam and for the underlying practice decision, since in the real setting the pharmacist would be reasoning from a specific drug against the enumerated categories.

guessability.note: This item can be shortcut without any legal analysis, by two independent routes. First, answer-polarity asymmetry: the call asks whether the protocol is acceptable, and exactly one of five options (C) says it is not, while A, B, D and E all validate the arrangement or excuse the pharmacist. In a single-best-answer set built around 'is this permissible?', a lone negative option among four permissive ones is a strong structural cue, and a test-wise candidate will select it on that basis alone. Second, the stem states the conclusion rather than supporting it: 'assigns the patient no preparation, storage, or handling role, sets no interval between the handover and the return, and runs the same way for every patient' are not neutral facts, they are three consecutive assertions that the handover is a pretence. A candidate who reads that clause has effectively been told the answer and needs only to match it to the option that says 'circumvents.' The distinctively Massachusetts content -- that c. 94C, s. 1(c) enumerates a closed list of pharmacist administration categories and that 247 CMR 9.01(2) is the express anti-circumvention hook -- is never required. Length and hedging are not cues here; C is mid-length and the options are of comparable register, so the guessability comes from polarity and from the conclusion-laden stem, not from surface wording.

potential_defect.note: The item is legally sound and, on my independent solve, correctly answerable as C; I found no error of law and no second defensible key. The defects are item-quality defects that would depress discrimination. (1) Guessability is high for the two structural reasons recorded above -- a single negative option among five, and a stem that asserts rather than supplies the pretext conclusion. (2) Distractor B is eliminable from the stem's own facts and contributes almost no discrimination, so the effective option count is four. (3) The stem stipulates away the jurisdiction-specific legal step. Because it hands the candidate 'Massachusetts does not authorize a pharmacist to administer this,' the item never requires knowledge of M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1(c), 105 CMR 700.001 or 105 CMR 700.003 -- which is the Massachusetts law actually at stake -- and reduces to a general inference about sham sequencing that a candidate with no Massachusetts knowledge can make. (4) Choice C's operative words ('indirectly circumvents') track 247 CMR 9.01(2)'s operative words ('directly or indirectly, to circumvent') closely enough that a candidate who recalls the regulation matches on wording rather than on analysis; that is acceptable in isolation but compounds the cueing above. I did not find any defect that makes the item unanswerable or wrongly keyed on my reading.

responses.blind_reasoning: Step 1 -- is the medication even within the Massachusetts controlled-substance framework? Yes. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 3(a)(6) puts every prescription drug not already in Schedules I through V into Schedule VI, so an ordinary prescription injectable is a 'controlled substance' in Massachusetts and the c. 94C machinery applies. Step 2 -- who may lawfully administer? M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1 defines 'Administer' as the direct application of a controlled substance to the body of a patient by a closed list: a practitioner; a nurse at a practitioner's direction; a registered pharmacist only when acting under DPH regulations for mental health and substance use disorder medications at a prescribing practitioner's direction, or under a prescription for testosterone for gender-affirming care, or under a prescription for treatment or prevention of sexually transmitted infections or prevention of HIV; or an ultimate user at a practitioner's direction. 105 CMR 700.001 carries the same closed structure, and 105 CMR 700.003(6) adds a separate, conditioned authority for designated immunizations, expressed as 'dispense by administration.' Massachusetts pharmacist administration authority is therefore enumerated and bounded, not general. The stem stipulates that this medication sits outside it. Step 3 -- does the choreography change who administers? No. The operative act under the s. 1 definition is the direct application of the substance to the patient's body, and the stem says the pharmacist performs the injection. The patient's momentary custody of an unopened syringe is not an application of anything to anyone; the s. 1(d) ultimate-user route would require the patient to inject themselves. So the pharmacist remains the administering party throughout, which disposes of choice B on the stem's own facts. Step 4 -- does the 'completed dispensing' label rescue it? No, and the statute cuts the other way. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1 defines 'Dispense' to include 'the prescribing and administering of a controlled substance,' so administration is a component of the dispensing chain rather than an alternative to it; characterizing the register handover as a finished dispensing does not detach the subsequent injection from the rules on who may administer. That disposes of choice A, and the same reasoning disposes of choice D: a valid prescription and a lawful dispensing establish authority to deliver the drug, not authority for this practitioner class to put it into the patient's body, which s. 1(c) grants only in the enumerated categories. Step 5 -- what is the affirmative prohibition? 247 CMR 9.01(2): 'A licensee may not process a prescription; dispense a drug, device, or other substance; or administer a controlled substance or vaccine in a manner which is intended, either directly or indirectly, to circumvent any law or regulation governing the practice of pharmacy.' The regulation is written precisely for this fact pattern -- it reaches indirect circumvention and it attaches to the manner in which the steps are arranged, not to their labels. The stem supplies the facts that establish the manner is pretextual: the patient gets no preparation, storage or handling role, no interval is set between handover and return, and the sequence is identical for every patient, so the handover has no clinical or operational function other than to manufacture a paper record that the drug had been dispensed before the injection. 247 CMR 9.01(4) independently requires the pharmacist to practise within the recognized pharmacist scope of practice, which the injection would exceed. Step 6 -- can the individual pharmacist point at the protocol's author? No. 247 CMR 10.03(1) authorizes discipline against 'an individual or entity licensed or registered by the Board,' and its enumerated grounds include (f) engaging in conduct beyond the authorized scope of a pharmacist, (b) violating state statutes or regulations related to the practice of the profession, (e) misconduct in the practice of the profession, and (l) conduct with the capacity or potential to deceive. Responsibility is personal to the licensee who performs the act; that a corporate author designed the sequence is at most additional exposure for that author and for the Manager of Record under 247 CMR 9.23, not a transfer of the staff pharmacist's own liability. That disposes of choice E. Conclusion: the protocol is impermissible because arranging the steps this way indirectly circumvents the administration restriction, which is choice C.
